document.title: Response of American Municipal Power, Inc

pages.text:
UNITED STATES OF AMERICA 
BEFORE THE 
FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION 
 
PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., et al. 
) 
Docket No. EL25-49-000 
 
) 
 
Large Loads Co-Located at 
  Generating Facilities 
) 
) 
Docket No. AD24-11-000 
 
) 
 
Constellation Energy Generation, LLC 
 
  v. 
 
) 
) 
) 
) 
Docket No. EL25-20-000 
   (Consolidated) 
PJM Interconnection, L.L.C. 
) 
 
 
RESPONSE OF 
AMERICAN MUNICIPAL POWER, INC. 
 
Pursuant to the procedures established in the Federal Energy Regulatory 
Commission’s (“Commission” or “FERC”) February 20, 2025 order in the above-captioned 
proceedings,1 American Municipal Power, Inc. (“AMP”) hereby addresses the issues 
raised in the Show Cause Order and responds to the filings submitted by PJM 
Interconnection, L.L.C. (“PJM”) and certain PJM Transmission Owners on those matters.2 
I. 
INTRODUCTION AND SUMMARY OF POSITION 
In response to a complaint filed by Constellation Energy Generation, LLC 
(“Constellation”)3 and the record developed in connection with the Commission’s 
November 1, 2024 technical conference on large loads co-located at generating facilities,4 
                                            
1  PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 190 FERC ¶ 61,115 (2025) (“Show Cause Order”). 
2  See Indicated PJM Transmission Owners, Answer, Docket Nos. EL25-49-000, et al. (March 24, 2025) 
(“Indicated PJM TOs Answer”); PJM, Answer, Docket Nos. EL25-49-000, et al. (March 24, 2025) (“PJM 
Answer”); Public Service Electric and Gas Co., Response, Docket Nos. EL25-49-000, et al. (March 24, 
2025) (“PSE&G Response”). 
3  Constellation, Complaint, Docket No. EL25-20-000 (Nov. 22, 2024) (“Constellation Complaint”). 
4  Large Loads Co-Located at Generating Facilities, Docket No. AD24-11-000 (“Co-Located Load 
Technical Conference”).

2 
the Commission’s Show Cause Order found that PJM’s Open Access Transmission Tariff 
(“Tariff”) “appears to be unjust and unreasonable or unduly discriminatory or preferential 
because it does not contain provisions addressing with sufficient clarity or consistency 
the rates, terms, and conditions of service that apply to co-location arrangements.”5 The 
Commission accordingly initiated a new proceeding under section 206 of the Federal 
Power Act (“FPA”), consolidated the new proceeding with the Constellation Complaint 
and Co-Located Load Technical Conference dockets, and directed PJM and the PJM 
Transmission Owners: (1) to show cause as to why the PJM Tariff remains just and 
reasonable and not unduly discriminatory or preferential; or (2) explain what Tariff 
changes “would remedy the Commission’s identified concerns if the Commission were to 
determine that the Tariff has in fact become unjust and unreasonable or unduly 
discriminatory or preferential.”6 The Commission identified a number questions that PJM 
and Transmission Owners should address in responding to the order.7  
PJM, while maintaining that its Tariff remains just and reasonable, identified eight 
“options” for the treatment of large load co-location.8 In addition to the answer filed by 
PJM, most PJM Transmission Owners submitted a joint answer to the Show Cause Order, 
while other Transmission Owners, including PSE&G, filed individual responses. 
AMP supports the answer filed by the Indicated PJM Transmission Owners. AMP 
agrees that the existing PJM Tariff is just and reasonable, although additional clarification 
                                            
5  Show Cause Order at P 74. For purposes of the Show Cause Order, the Commission defines co-located 
load as “a configuration through which end-use customer load is physically connected to the facilities of 
an existing or planned generation unit on the interconnection customer’s side of the point of 
interconnection to the PJM transmission system.” Id. P 3. 
6  Id. P 87.  
7  Id. P 88. 
8  See PJM Answer at 9-20 & Exh. A.

3 
concerning the treatment of co-located load may be beneficial.9 As the Indicated PJM 
Transmission Owners explain, it is important that load co-located behind the 
interconnection point of an adjacent generator in PJM is considered Network Load (or 
load taking Point-to-Point Transmission Service) to avoid unjust and unreasonable cost-
shifting and to promote reliable transmission planning and resource adequacy. 
While AMP supports the answer of the Indicated PJM Transmission Owners, AMP 
is filing this response to emphasize the continuing reasonableness of the PJM Tariff’s 
treatment of load served by Behind the Meter Generation (“BTMG”) and Non-Retail 
BTMG, as those terms are defined in the Tariff.10 Specifically, the PJM Tariff allows 
certain Network Load served by BTMG to be netted for purposes of calculating 
transmission, and certain other charges.11 These Tariff provisions conform to cost 
causation principles – as the Commission found in approving them12 – and provide 
meaningful benefits to electric consumers. Even if the Commission agrees with PJM that 
“[t]he extent to which netting could or should apply to co-located data center load is not 
clear at this time,”13 there is no reason to revisit the existing Tariff framework allowing 
BTMG netting. Indeed, PJM correctly asserts that its existing Tariff remains just and 
reasonable.14 Any action taken by the Commission in this proceeding should avoid 
                                            
9  See, e.g., Indicated PJM TOs Answer at 2. 
10  In this response, AMP’s references to BTMG should be read to include Non-Retail BTMG unless 
otherwise indicated. 
11  See PJM Tariff, §§ 34.2 and 34.3; see also, e.g., PJM Manual 14D, Appendix A at p. 179 (“The purpose 
of these rules is to permit market participants operating Behind-the-Meter Generation (BTMG) to receive 
the associated benefits. These benefits are recognized by allowing such generation to net for the 
purposes of calculating transmission, capacity, ancillary services, and administrative fee charges.”); 
PJM Answer at 11-12, 34-37. 
12  See PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 107 FERC ¶ 61,113, at P 28, reh’g denied, 108 FERC ¶ 61,302 (2004). 
13  PJM Answer at 35. 
14  Id. at 4, 32.

4 
prejudice to entities that have relied on the longstanding provisions allowing for netting of 
Network Load served by BTMG. 
Although PSE&G’s response persuasively documents the benefits of the PJM 
Tariff’s existing BTMG netting provisions,15 PSE&G incorrectly suggests (as have other 
parties in these consolidated proceedings) that treating large loads that co-locate behind 
an adjacent generator’s point of interconnection differently than loads eligible for netting 
under the BTMG provisions of the Tariff would necessarily raise undue discrimination 
concerns.16 The record does not support a finding that co-location arrangements for large 
loads (such as data centers) that appear to be the focus of PSE&G’s discrimination 
concerns17 would meet the existing requirements for BTMG and/or Non-Retail BTMG 
netting, or that co-located load is otherwise similarly situated to load served by BTMG 
and eligible for netting under the PJM Tariff. 
II. 
INTEREST OF AMP 
AMP is a nonprofit Ohio corporation with members in Delaware, Indiana, Kentucky, 
Maryland, Michigan, Ohio, Pennsylvania, Virginia, and West Virginia, the majority of 
which are load-serving entities within the PJM region. To meet those members’ load 
service responsibilities, AMP purchases transmission and related services from PJM and 
also purchases and sells electricity products in the markets operated by PJM.18 
                                            
15  See PSE&G Response at 18 & Exh. 1. 
16  See, e.g., id. at 13-14. 
17  See, e.g., id. at 2 (arguing for an approach that, inter alia, “preserves co-location as a viable option to 
support data center development in New Jersey and elsewhere in PJM”). 
18  AMP Transmission LLC (“AMP Transmission”), a wholly owned subsidiary of AMP, is a PJM 
Transmission Owner. AMP Transmission is a signatory to the Indicated PJM Transmission Owners’ 
Answer.

5 
III. 
RESPONSE 
A. 
AMP supports the answer of the Indicated PJM Transmission Owners. 
The Indicated PJM Transmission Owners correctly assert that the current PJM 
Tariff remains just and reasonable19 – a position that is echoed by PJM itself.20 As the 
Transmission Owners observe, “[c]o-located load can and does fit within the current 
constructs for providing transmission service” under the pro forma open access 
transmission tariff and the PJM Tariff.21 In particular, load served under co-location 
arrangements should be treated as Network Load (or load served by Point-to-Point 
Service). Treating co-located load as Network Load or load served by Point-to-Point 
Service avoids unjust and unreasonable transmission cost-shifting,22 while promoting 
reliable transmission planning and resource adequacy.23 
The responses filed by PJM and the Indicated PJM Transmission Owners do not 
support a finding that the existing PJM Tariff is unjust and unreasonable (they assert the 
opposite), and, thus, they provide no basis to modify the Tariff under FPA section 206.24 
Like the Indicated PJM Transmission Owners, however, AMP is amenable to further 
discussion and guidance regarding possible Tariff changes to clarify the treatment of co-
located load. The Indicated PJM Transmission Owners, for example, suggest a 
reasonable definition of “Co-located Load” that would appropriately clarify how co-located 
                                            
19  Indicated PJM TOs Answer at 2. 
20  PJM Answer at 4, 32. 
21  Indicated PJM TOs Answer at 2. 
22  See id. at 3. 
23  See id. at 3-4. 
24  16 U.S.C. § 824e; see also, e.g., Emera Maine v. FERC, 854 F.3d 9, 24-25 (D.C. Cir. 2017).

6 
arrangements fit within the existing PJM Tariff framework.25 The definition suggested by 
the Indicated PJM Transmission Owners would appropriately preserve the current 
treatment of load served by BTMG and Non-Retail BTMG.26  
Regardless of whether the Commission concludes that the PJM Tariff should be 
modified to address co-located arrangements, however, there is no basis to modify the 
current BTMG netting provisions in the PJM Tariff, as discussed below.27 
B. 
The existing PJM Tariff provisions addressing BTMG netting should 
be retained. 
1. 
The BTMG netting provisions were adopted in conformance 
with cost causation principles. 
Under sections 34.2 and 34.3 of the PJM Tariff, load served by BTMG is, subject 
to certain requirements and limitations, eligible to be excluded – or netted – from a 
Network Customer’s daily load for purposes of calculating charges for Network Service 
and other PJM charges.28 This does not mean that load served by BTMG and Non-Retail 
                                            
25  See Indicated PJM TOs Answer at 9. 
26  Specifically, the suggested definition of Co-located Load would distinguish between the generation 
resources adjacent to load in a co-located load arrangement and generation resources that meet the 
definition of BTMG. See id. 
27  See Show Cause Order at P 88, question a.iv (“Parties may also address how co-located loads are 
similar to or disparate from other types of arrangements where load and generation share the same 
point of interconnection (such as Behind the Meter Generation as defined in PJM’s Tariff or non-retail 
behind the meter generation) and should consider how any proposed replacement rate would interact 
with these other arrangements.”). 
28  The PJM Tariff defines Behind the Meter Generation as:  
a generation unit that delivers energy to load without using the Transmission 
System or any distribution facilities (unless the entity that owns or leases the 
distribution facilities has consented to such use of the distribution facilities and 
such consent has been demonstrated to the satisfaction of the Office of the 
Interconnection); provided, however, that Behind The Meter Generation does not 
include (i) at any time, any portion of such generating unit’s capacity that is 
designated as a Generation Capacity Resource; or (ii) in an hour, any portion of 
the output of such generating unit that is sold to another entity for consumption at 
another electrical location or into the PJM Interchange Energy Market. 
 
The Tariff, in turn, defines Non-Retail BTMG as “Behind the Meter Generation that is used by municipal 
electric systems, electric cooperatives, or electric distribution companies to serve load.”

7 
BTMG is not considered Network Load; the relevant netting provisions are only available 
to Network Customers, and as PJM explains, “all load served by BTM Generation must 
be designated Network Load.”29 
Netting of Network Load served by BTMG conforms to cost causation principles. 
Load eligible for netting under sections 34.2 and 34.3 of the PJM Tariff is served by 
generation that, by definition, delivers energy to load without using the transmission 
system.30 In accepting the original BTMG netting provisions in the PJM Tariff, the 
Commission specifically observed that PJM’s “charges for the use of PJM’s transmission 
system should be allocated to network customers based on a network customer’s actual 
use of PJM's system, consistent with the principle of cost causation.”31 The Commission 
also agreed that the BTMG netting provisions were consistent with its policy of 
encouraging demand response programs,32 as PJM observed that its proposal would 
“encourage the use of behind the meter generation during times of scarcity and high 
prices.”33 
The PJM Tariff provisions addressing netting of load served by Non-Retail BTMG 
were adopted in a 2005 settlement agreement,34 reached after the Commission found 
that “PJM’s current tariff that excludes from the BTM program all generation that is 
connected to load through a distribution system may not be just and reasonable, and may 
                                            
29  PJM Answer at 35. 
30  See supra note 28. 
31  PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 107 FERC ¶ 61,113 at P 28 (quoting Occidental Chem. Corp. v. PJM, 102 
FERC ¶ 61,275 (2003) (internal quotes omitted)). 
32  Id. P 27. 
33  Id. P 6. 
34  See PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 113 FERC ¶ 61,279 (2005).

8 
be unjust, unreasonable, unduly discriminatory or preferential or otherwise unlawful.”35 
Section 34.3 of the Tariff thus extends the same netting availability, subject to certain 
conditions, to BTMG used by municipal electric systems, electric cooperatives, or electric 
distribution companies to serve load, consistent with the cost causation principles 
recognized by the Commission in accepting the original BTMG netting provisions. 
2. 
The BTMG Tariff provisions provide benefits while protecting 
against adverse impacts. 
AMP and a number of its load-serving utility members rely on generating units that 
qualify as Non-Retail BTMG. These resources, while generally small, provide significant 
benefits to the consumers of AMP’s member utilities. Consistent with the original 
purposes of the BTMG netting approach, the PJM Tariff allows consumers to avoid costs 
that do not reflect their actual use of the transmission system. The transmission cost 
mitigation impacts of Non-Retail BTMG netting are extremely important to AMP’s 
members at a time of sharply increasing transmission expenses in the PJM region. The 
answer filed by PSE&G documents similar benefits for customers in New Jersey, 
including universities, government agencies, manufacturers, and other consumers.36 
Other technical conference commenters cited similar benefits.37 
Continuing to facilitate BTMG resources is also likely to provide reliability benefits. 
As noted above, one of PJM’s original justifications in proposing BTMG netting was that 
it would “encourage the use of behind the meter generation during times of scarcity and 
                                            
35  PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 112 FERC ¶ 61,034, at P 18 (2005). 
36  PSE&G Response at 18 & Exh. 1. 
37  See, e.g., Northeastern Rural Electric Membership Corporation, Post-Technical Conference Comments, 
Docket No. AD24-11-000 (Dec. 9, 2024).

9 
high prices.”38 Tariff provisions that encourage the operation of BTMG generation as a 
form of demand response at times of scarcity are likely to enhance reliability. Indeed, in 
its answer, PJM describes current efforts to facilitate increased use of small generators 
to promote resource adequacy, explaining that “PJM is also exploring with regulators and 
generators opportunities to leverage at least 50 hours (or more) of diesel back-up 
generator service to enhance the available demand response portfolio.”39 In addition to 
demand response benefits, BTMG installations can provide a source of emergency 
backup generation for some customers should a major outage occur. 
The PJM Tariff, moreover, includes a number of conditions on Non-Retail BTMG 
netting specifically designed to address initial PJM reservations that adverse reliability 
impacts could result from greater levels of BTMG if the netting rules were extended to 
municipals and cooperatives.40 Specifically, even though the definition of BTMG (and by 
extension Non-Retail BTMG), excludes any portion of “the generating unit’s capacity that 
is designated as a Generation Capacity Resource,” Non-Retail BTMG must operate 
during the first ten occurrences of Maximum Generation Emergency conditions each year 
in the zone where the unit is located.41 Further, section 34.3 of the Tariff caps the total 
amount of Non-Retail BTMG in the PJM Region in any specific year, and sets a maximum 
ceiling of 3,000 MW absent a filing by PJM to expand the cap or modify the netting rules.42 
                                            
38  PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 107 FERC ¶ 61,113 at P 6. 
39  PJM Answer at 9. 
40  See PJM, Offer of Settlement, Docket No. EL05-127-000, Explanatory Statement at 9-10 (Oct. 24, 
2005); see also PJM Answer at 13 n.5. 
41  PJM Tariff, Schedule 15. 
42  PJM Tariff, § 34.3; PJM, Offer of Settlement, Docket No. EL05-127-000, Explanatory Statement at 6-7.

10 
3. 
The record provides no basis to revisit the current PJM Tariff 
provisions addressing BTMG. 
AMP strongly agrees with PSE&G’s admonition that the Commission “should allow 
existing BTMG customers to continue to net and should take no action that would 
disadvantage these existing customers.”43 Indeed, as discussed above, the PJM and 
Transmission Owner responses do not provide any basis for finding that the existing 
BTMG netting provisions are subject to modification under FPA section 206 as unjust and 
unreasonable, or unduly discriminatory or preferential.   
While maintaining that its Tariff remains just and reasonable, PJM discordantly 
suggests that “discussions in the record regarding PJM’s BTM Generation rules raise 
questions about the status of those rules,”44 and PJM states that it is “open to exploring . 
. . whether the 20-year-old method of allocating costs pursuant to the BTM Generation 
netting rules remains consistent with cost causation principles.”45 PJM does not provide 
any citations to the “discussions in the record” that supposedly call the existing netting 
provisions into question, nor does it identify any reason why the longstanding practice of 
netting loads served by BTMG might no longer be “consistent with cost causation 
principles.”46 As the Commission found in originally approving the BTMG netting 
provisions in the PJM Tariff, those provisions allocate transmission system costs to 
Network Customers based on their actual use of PJM’s system, “consistent with the 
principle of cost causation.”47 That observation is as true today as it was in 2004. If 
                                            
43  PSE&G Response at 6; see also, e.g., Northeastern Rural Electric Membership Corporation, Post-
Technical Conference Comments, Docket No. AD24-11-000 (Dec. 9, 2024). 
44  PJM Answer at 36. 
45  Id. at 36-37. 
46  Id. 
47  PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 107 FERC ¶ 61,113 at P 28.

11 
anything, the longstanding nature of the netting provisions is a reason to retain, not revisit 
them, given the reliance interests of PJM market participants in the existing rules.48  
PJM suggests that large load co-location arrangements might fall within the Tariff’s 
existing BTMG netting provisions, and PJM’s “Option 3” is based on this premise.49 PJM 
nonetheless expresses concern that “the BTM Generation paradigm does not fit co-
location arrangements particularly well because it was not designed with large load co-
location in mind,”50 and PJM ultimately observes that “[t]he extent to which netting could 
or should apply to co-located data center load is not clear at this time.”51 AMP agrees that 
the existing BTMG provisions were not designed with large co-located loads in mind, but 
concerns about whether and how large loads co-locating at existing generation units fit 
within the existing BTMG netting framework is not a reason to upset the existing 
framework, which was adopted in conformance with cost causation principles, and which 
is reflected in a Tariff that PJM insists remains just and reasonable. 
PSE&G correctly argues that the Commission should avoid adversely impacting 
entities that rely on the existing BTMG provisions of the PJM Tariff, but goes on to suggest 
that it would be unduly discriminatory to treat co-located “behind the meter load” 
differently than load served by BTMG for netting purposes.52 The Commission has 
                                            
48  See, e.g., Dep’t of Homeland Sec. v. Regents of the Univ. of Cal., 591 U.S. 1, 30 (2020) (explaining that 
an agency “must be cognizant that longstanding policies may have engendered serious reliance 
interests that must be taken into account.” (cleaned up)). 
49  See, e.g., PJM Answer at 11-13; see also id. at 34 (“The co-located load arrangements at issue here, 
large data centers, could be viewed as similar to BTM Generation that currently exists under PJM’s Tariff 
(as reflected in Exhibit A, Option 3).”). 
50  Id. at 34; see also id. at 13 (discussing PJM’s Option 3 and noting that “[w]hile this option is already 
available under the Tariff, it was conceived for, and has been implemented for, substantially smaller 
loads (like a large warehouse with solar panels) and not on the scale of large data centers.”). 
51  Id. at 35. 
52  PSE&G Response at 13-14.

12 
observed, however, that “different co-location arrangements are likely to use or benefit 
from the transmission system in different ways depending on how they are configured 
and, moreover, that those different configurations will themselves likely have different 
impacts on the transmission system.”53 PSE&G has not demonstrated that large co-
located data center loads that appear to be the focus of its discrimination concerns54 
would be able to comply with the existing requirements for BTMG or that these loads 
would otherwise be similarly situated to load served by BTMG behind the load’s point of 
interconnection, particularly given PSE&G’s acknowledgement that there may be a 
variety of co-located load configurations.55 
As a threshold matter, any co-located load claiming to be similarly situated to load 
served by BTMG must, at a minimum, be designated Network Load, as only Network 
Load is eligible for BTMG netting.56 The PJM Tariff also specifically defines BTMG as “a 
generation unit that delivers energy to load without using the Transmission System.”57 
While PSE&G asserts that “[f]rom a technical perspective, there is no material distinction 
between a BTM load arrangement relative to a BTMG arrangement,”58 generating plants 
interconnected to the transmission system and serving large co-located loads rely on the 
transmission system to deliver energy to load in a manner that BTMG connected behind 
a load meter does not. For example, as Indicated PJM Transmission Owners observe, 
                                            
53  Show Cause Order at P 76. 
54  See, e.g., PSE&G Response at 2 (arguing for an approach that, inter alia, “preserves co-location as a 
viable option to support data center development in New Jersey and elsewhere in PJM”). 
55  See, e.g., id. at 5. To the extent that participants in a co-located load arrangement believe it is eligible 
for netting under sections 34.2 and 34.3 of the PJM Tariff, they can seek to qualify under those provisions 
by meeting all the criteria. See Indicated PJM TOs Response, Attachment A at 4 n.6. 
56  See, e.g., PJM Answer at 35 (“all load served by BTM Generation must be designated Network Load.”). 
57  PJM, Tariff, Definitions A-B (emphasis added). 
58  PSE&G Response at 15.

13 
nuclear units are required to be interconnected to the transmission grid, and, thus would 
necessarily rely directly on the transmission grid to serve co-located load.59 In contrast, 
as PJM notes, BTMG netting “was conceived for, and has been implemented for, 
substantially smaller loads (like a large warehouse with solar panels) and not on the scale 
of large data centers.”60 These on-site generators, the Commission agreed, do not rely 
on the integrated transmission system (or even the distribution system) to deliver energy 
to load.61 The Non-Retail BTMG provisions of the PJM Tariff were later adopted, as 
discussed above, in response to Commission concerns about treating distribution-
connected generation differently than on-site generation, given that such generators also 
may not rely on the integrated transmission system to serve load.62 Indeed, BTMG may 
even be able to serve as a source of emergency backup generation during a grid outage. 
Thus, while, as Commissioner Rosner noted, new co-located load proposals may 
be the “inverse” of traditional BTMG arrangements,63 the Commissioner’s observation 
only serves to highlight that the arrangements are not the same, and, thus, may warrant 
different treatment.64 Regardless of whether the Commission agrees that co-located load 
arrangements should be entitled to some form of netting, however, the Commission 
should preserve the current BTMG and Non-Retail BTMG netting provisions in the PJM 
Tariff. 
                                            
59  See Indicated PJM TOs Answer at 13. 
60  PJM Answer at 13.  
61  See, e.g., PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 107 FERC ¶ 61,113 at P 4. 
62  PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 112 FERC ¶ 61,034 at PP 15-19. 
63  See PSE&G Response at 16 (citing Technical Conference Transcript at 14). 
64  See also PJM Answer at 36.

14 
IV. 
CONCLUSION 
WHEREFORE, for the foregoing reasons, American Municipal Power, Inc. 
respectfully asks the Commission to consider these comments in these dockets. 
Respectfully submitted,
